questions.stem: Which instrument suits measuring a small object's dimensions most precisely?

options.text: a micrometer
options.explanation: Its 0.001 mm resolution is the finest of the three.

options.text: a 30 cm ruler
options.explanation: Its 1 mm resolution is the coarsest.

options.text: a digital balance
options.explanation: The balance measures mass, not length.

options.text: a measuring cylinder
options.explanation: That reads liquid volumes.

questions.stem: What is the dependent variable in the regular-objects experiment?

options.text: the ruler's resolution
options.explanation: Resolution is fixed by the instrument.

options.text: the mass of the object
options.explanation: Mass answers to the changed shape or volume.

options.text: the type of shape or volume
options.explanation: That is the independent variable.

options.text: the density of water
options.explanation: Water is not part of experiment 1.

questions.stem: Why are the dimension measurements repeated and averaged?

options.text: because the balance requires three readings
options.explanation: The balance reading is taken once per object.

options.text: to change the object's true volume
options.explanation: Repetition reveals the value; it never changes the object.

options.text: to reduce the random error in the length readings
options.explanation: Averaging evens out the scatter of single readings.

options.text: to fix any zero error on the balance
options.explanation: Zero errors are systematic and need re-zeroing, not averaging.

questions.stem: Which sequence states the regular-objects method correctly?

options.text: fill the eureka can, lower the object, read the displacement
options.explanation: That is the irregular-objects technique.

options.text: zero the balance with liquid aboard, then weigh
options.explanation: The balance is zeroed empty, never loaded with liquid.

options.text: measure the volume directly with a micrometer
options.explanation: A micrometer reads lengths, not volumes.

options.text: weigh the object, measure its dimensions, average repeats, calculate density
options.explanation: Mass, dimensions, repeats, then the equation.

questions.stem: After the volume is rebuilt from the dimensions, what completes the density determination?

options.text: divide the averaged mass by the volume
options.explanation: ρ = m ÷ V closes the practical.

options.text: multiply the mass by the volume
options.explanation: The equation divides.

options.text: subtract the volume from the mass
options.explanation: Subtracting unlike quantities is meaningless.

options.text: compare the mass with water's density alone
options.explanation: The division by the object's own volume is required.

questions.stem: State the aim of the regular-objects experiment.
questions.modelAnswer: The experiment determines the densities of regular objects from their measured dimensions and their mass.

questions.stem: State which three instruments can take the dimension measurements, in decreasing size suitability.
questions.modelAnswer: The 30 cm ruler serves larger objects, the vernier calipers smaller ones, and the micrometer the smallest objects.

questions.stem: Explain why the digital balance reading is taken before any dimension work begins.
questions.modelAnswer: The mass is a single direct reading best taken cleanly at the start, so the object is weighed first and its dimensions gathered afterwards. Sequencing the weighing first also keeps handling from transferring moisture or grease that would bias the mass.

questions.stem: A student measures a cube's edge three times: 10 mm, 11 mm and 10 mm. State the averaged edge and explain the benefit of averaging.
questions.modelAnswer: The averaged edge is (10 + 11 + 10) ÷ 3 ≈ 10.3 mm, and averaging steadies the random scatter of single readings so the volume — and hence the density — rests on a fairer value.

questions.stem: What does the volume of displaced water equal?

options.text: half the object's volume
options.explanation: The displacement is complete, not partial.

options.text: the volume of the submerged object
options.explanation: Displacement hands over the object's volume exactly.

options.text: the mass of the object
options.explanation: Mass comes from the balance.

options.text: the density of the water
options.explanation: Density is not what the spout delivers.

questions.stem: Why must the measuring cylinder sit below the spout before the object goes in?

options.text: so the can can be emptied first
options.explanation: Emptying the cylinder is a separate preparatory step.

options.text: so the water warms to room temperature
options.explanation: Temperature is not the concern here.

options.text: so none of the displaced water is lost before it is read
options.explanation: Every drop of displacement must reach the cylinder.

options.text: so the object has somewhere to land
options.explanation: The object goes into the can, not the cylinder.

questions.stem: What is the dependent variable in the irregular-objects experiment?

options.text: the type of irregular shape or mass
options.explanation: That is the independent variable.

options.text: the can's overflow rate
options.explanation: Overflow is preparatory, not the measured outcome.

options.text: the density of the object
options.explanation: Density is the final calculation, not the variable read.

options.text: the volume of displaced water
options.explanation: Displacement answers to each new shape or mass.

questions.stem: Why lower the object gently rather than drop it?

options.text: dropping splashes water out, giving an incorrect volume reading
options.explanation: Splash losses corrupt the displacement.

options.text: the object might dissolve
options.explanation: Dissolving is not the cited risk.

options.text: gentle objects displace more water
options.explanation: Displacement depends on volume, not on entry speed.

options.text: the spout closes when startled
options.explanation: Nothing closes; physics is not sentimental.

questions.stem: Which extra step does the irregular-object method need that the regular-object method does not?

options.text: using the density equation
options.explanation: Both methods end in the same equation.

options.text: collecting displaced water from a eureka can
options.explanation: Displacement replaces the geometry step.

options.text: weighing the object on a balance
options.explanation: Both methods weigh the object.

options.text: repeating readings and averaging
options.explanation: Both methods repeat and average.

questions.stem: State the aim of the irregular-objects experiment.
questions.modelAnswer: The experiment finds the densities of irregular objects through a displacement technique.

questions.stem: State what must be done with the measuring cylinder just before lowering the object in.
questions.modelAnswer: An empty measuring cylinder is placed below the spout, and the cylinder is emptied of any earlier overflow before the object enters.

questions.stem: Explain why the eureka can is filled until water overflows and then allowed to settle before the object is added.
questions.modelAnswer: Filling to overflowing guarantees the can is full to the spout's lip, so any later displacement escapes only through the spout. Allowing it to settle means the pre-experiment drips have finished; without that, stray drips would join the object's true displacement and inflate the reading.

questions.stem: An irregular object of mass 240 g displaces 30 cm³ of water. Calculate its density in g/cm³.
questions.modelAnswer: Density = 240 ÷ 30 = 8 g/cm³, since the displaced volume equals the object's volume.

questions.stem: How is the liquid's mass obtained?

options.text: weigh the liquid in an open beaker only
options.explanation: The method weighs the cylinder, empty and filled.

options.text: multiply the volume by the density
options.explanation: That would need the density already known.

options.text: subtract the empty cylinder's mass from the filled cylinder's reading
options.explanation: The difference isolates the liquid.

options.text: read it directly from the cylinder's scale
options.explanation: The scale reads volume, not mass.

questions.stem: Why is the balance zeroed with the empty cylinder on it?

options.text: to reduce the random error of pouring
options.explanation: Random error is the repeats' job.

options.text: because the balance cannot read a cylinder
options.explanation: The balance reads anything placed on it.

options.text: to warm the balance up
options.explanation: Warm-up is not the cited reason.

options.text: to remove the systematic offset the cylinder's own mass would add
options.explanation: Zeroing kills the constant bias; repeats cannot.

questions.stem: Which hazard belongs in this practical's safety notes alongside its glassware?

options.text: pouring water onto the electric balance risks a shock
options.explanation: The safety notes warn exactly this.

options.text: the eureka can's steam burns
options.explanation: No steam appears in a density practical.

options.text: radioactive samples under test
options.explanation: Nothing radioactive is involved.

options.text: pressure vessels bursting
options.explanation: No pressurised equipment is used.

questions.stem: Which error family do repeat-and-average fixes address?

options.text: equipment failure
options.explanation: Broken equipment needs replacing, not averaging.

options.text: random error
options.explanation: Averaging evens out scatter in both directions.

options.text: systematic error
options.explanation: Systematic offsets need re-zeroing or recalibration.

options.text: human dishonesty
options.explanation: The fix is statistical, not moral.

questions.stem: A student records 50 g for the empty cylinder and 130 g with liquid aboard. The liquid's mass is

options.explanation: That is the cylinder alone.
That adds instead of subtracting.
130 − 50 = 80 grams of liquid.
That includes the cylinder.

questions.stem: State the mass-difference sentence used in the liquid experiment.
questions.modelAnswer: Mass of liquid equals the mass of the cylinder with liquid minus the mass of the empty cylinder.

questions.stem: State one systematic-error fix and one random-error fix from these experiments.
questions.modelAnswer: Zeroing the digital balance before readings fixes a systematic error; repeating measurements and taking averages fixes random error.

questions.stem: Explain why the measuring cylinder must never sit on the balance while water is poured into it.
questions.modelAnswer: The balance is an electrical instrument and spilled water inside it can cause an electric shock, so the cylinder is filled away from the balance and only then placed aboard for the reading.

questions.stem: A student obtains liquid masses of 78 g, 82 g and 80 g across three repeats. State the averaged mass and the density if the poured volume was 100 cm³.
questions.modelAnswer: The averaged mass is (78 + 82 + 80) ÷ 3 = 80 g, and the density is 80 ÷ 100 = 0.8 g/cm³.
